analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in Codd against Velger. Mr. Ritchland, I think you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court? We come here by certiorari to the Second Circuit Court of Appeals in a matter of great concern to my city and a matter which I suggest is and should be of concern to every government official who has it in his power to appoint and to remove non-tenured officials who serve at his will and discretion. The issue here presented in the narrow sense as I see it is may a non-tenured municipal employee who can be dismissed at will be dismissed without a hearing when his first nail record contains derogatory matter which can be examined by prospective employers only with the written permission of the dismissed employee. And in the broader sense, and that arises out of the nature of the opinion of the Second Court of Appeals here, can such an employee be so dismissed when his record might at some time in the future be examined by interested prospective employees with or without such express permission? Well, how would they get it without his permission? I thought you said they must have his permission. Under the specific ruling of this case, under the specific facts of this case, permission was granted, and it was as a result of permission being granted that the inspection was permitted. However, there is implicit, and I think to a considerable degree explicit, in the opinion of the Second Court of Appeals, which incidentally was decided before this court decided Paul and Bishop last term. That goes quite beyond that. It's not realistic. When a man applies for a job and he says, do you work for the city of New York? He said, yes. He said, why did you leave? And he says, I won't tell you. He won't get employed, will he? That's quite true. That's quite true. And this is one of the... The permission is just... This is one of the necessary incidents of exempt positions, of positions to which people are appointed at will. I suggest it. I suggest this example, and I've suggested it in my brief. And I think it highlights what our problem is here. Supposing a justice of this court has a confidential clerk in whom he has lost confidence because he believes, if you please, that he has a loose tongue and talks out of court. And so terminates him. He then applies to the chief judge of our court of appeals for a position as confidential clerk. And chief judge Brightail calls the justice of this court and says, what about this man? Under the ruling of this case, I submit, not only could the justice of this court not tell him, but there is doubt as to whether or not he was permitted to pick up the telephone to answer the call. Because if you please, he had given him no hearing. I'm talking about a policeman. I'm talking about a policeman. And I'm talking about, and I'm talking... I suggest, I suggest that the rule is broader than that. But if you brought, if you leave it to strictly to policemen and make a special exception so as to exempt this court and its justices... Civil service employees? I have 800 civil service employees in my office. Did the court of appeals... Many of which... Did the court of appeals limit its ruling to civil service employees? It did not. It did not purport to limit it to anyone. And during the first year, do I understand correctly, during the first year of probation, they can be dismissed for no reason. At any time. At any time. Because that is part of the appointing process, as a matter of fact. But it is the same... The law clerks on the highest court of New York or other courts in New York are on the same basis, I suppose. That is, they can be dismissed at any time. They can be dismissed at will. So during the first year... Just as your own confidential secretaries can be dismissed at will. Just as my own confidential assistants can be dismissed at will. During the first year, then, the law clerks are in about the same posture as a probationary employee. Exactly. Exactly. They are non-tenured. They have no property right in their position. And that is exactly what the situation is here. And I suggest that it is utterly impossible to properly operate a government in which confidential assistants are necessary, in which exempt personnel are necessary, under this kind of a ruling. And I suggest that the ruling is utterly inconsistent with the decisions of this court last term. was the Paul case and the Bishop case. Obviously, there was no property right possessed by Mr. Belgov in his job. Obviously, he held his job at the will of the appointing officer and he was dismissed. And the... He is not upsetting a right to due process before he was dismissed, is he? I suggest that he is not in time to due process unless his liberty is impinged. Right. I'm asking what the issue in this case is. The issue in this case is whether such a person can be so dismissed without violating his liberty. Oh, I thought the issue involved a disclosure of the personnel file subsequent to dismissal. No, no. The issue is whether or not such a person can be dismissed when his file is likely to be exposed without having previously enjoyed a hearing. And by hearing, I assume, a hearing with a full panoply of cross-examination and appearance by counsel. Right, but if his file had never been disclosed, would there be any case here today? If his file had never been, we wouldn't be here today. Right. No doubt about that. So disclosure... Well, we might have been here a year from now. We might have been here four years from now. But I'm talking about this case, which involves disclosure of the file. Is that correct? If there had been no disclosure, even though the policeman in this case invited disclosure by offering an authorization to his future employee, granting him permission to disclose, of course we wouldn't be here. But this is exactly what he did. And it's disclosure that therefore, as my brother Powell suggests, is the critical fact in this case. Oh, it is the potential of disclosure. No, the fact of disclosure. As I read the opinion of the Circuit Court of Appeals... Had there never been disclosure, and were there never disclosure, there would never be a cause of action with it. Well, of course not. How did it come to be disclosed? How did it come to be disclosed? It came to be disclosed when an application was made by the discharged employee to the Penn Central Police Department. They asked him... It's a private entity. It's a private entity. They asked him what his background was. He told them what his background was. They then procured from him a written authorization without which the police department would not have granted them any information. They took that to the police department, and the police department allowed them to see his record. So you said that he made the disclosure? Of course he made the disclosure, and as a matter of fact, the only public disclosure that has been made in this case has been made by my friend in this case by bringing this suit. Before that, there was no public disclosure. There was at most a private disclosure with the permission of the employee. Mr. Richland, if that argument is a complete answer to the case, I suppose you'd take the same position if the file showed he was guilty of murder. Well, of course. No matter what stigmatizing reason. Of course. And he has his remedy. If that is a false statement, and it is a deliberately false statement, he has his remedy in the state court. What's his remedy? His remedy is an action in defamation. But how does he find out what the file shows? If nobody finds out what the file shows, what difference does it make? Well, the practical problem is that if he does not grant access, he can't get another job. Not necessarily. I thought you conceded that earlier, that if he followed the practice of saying, no, I won't let you look at the, don't tell you why I was fired, he'll never get another job. It doesn't necessarily follow. There may be people that don't ask him. There may be people that don't care about what his record was in the police department. He had changed that three times in the last six minutes. Oh, I, I, I... You told me distinctly that you recognized that that was a problem. Didn't you? No, I'm sorry, but I, if that is the impression your honor got, then I have certainly misspoken. Well, that's the impression that Judge, Justice Clark had. He put it in his opinion. He said it was assumed that this man couldn't get a job without it. I don't think that assumption is valid anyway. You know, he can get jobs all over the place. There's nobody has, has ever disqualified him. He has never been disqualified from any of the various civil service lists in which he's been placed. The only other police agency to which he applied and on which he relies in an appendix to his, to, to his brief sent him a letter which says that, uh, we, which ends up by saying, we thank you for your interest in the Plainfield Police Division and wish you success in your future endeavors. And that's not any proof that he was rejected because of a failure to produce his records or anything else. And we're bound here by our record. Well, New York imposed no requirement that he had to disclose his record in order to get another job. Of course not. Those were requirements imposed by private employers. Of course not. Of course not. And I submit that... One other question, Mr. Richland. Is there any provision in your regulations for disclosure to the discharged employee of the matter that's given to third parties? In other words, could he have gotten access to the file himself? I believe he could have. I take it there's nothing in the record to show he made a request other than the written and derogatory that you kind of evasively... There is no direct proof that he offered such, that he made such a request. By the way, there is one strange aspect of this case that I think your honor should know. And that is that Mr. Belger was present at the trial before the trial justice and heard the statement of the Pennsylvania railroad personnel officer that said that he had read in his file that he put a gun to his head and sent to suicide. Mr. Belger did not take the stand to deny or dispute it. That fact has never been disputed. And this, it seems to me, shows how tenuous is this whole notion that the circumstance that there is information in a file that is derogatory of someone in itself requires that he not be dismissed without a hearing. Well, don't you think the state ought to have some reason to say it? Why should he go around and why should he be bound to disprove everything that anybody says? Well, I think... Does anybody... Is there any witnesses in this report? No. It's just a blanket statement. That's all. Isn't it... Isn't it... Isn't it something that he could have denied? Isn't it... Wasn't it put upon him to deny it? Why? Wasn't it put upon him to say that didn't happen at all? This is a pure invention. Why? Why is he obliged to deny it? Because he is a provisional employee and if he is dismissed he can be dismissed for no reason. He doesn't have any right not to be maligned? I don't... Of course he has a right not to be maligned. Of course he has a right not to be maligned. But is that... Is this the remedy? Is this the remedy? If he is maligned he has an action in tort. He has an action for slander. He has an action for libel. As this court held last term the right to reputation is not protected by the 14th Amendment. It is not one of the liberties that is protected. Mr. Wilson, getting back to the New Jersey one. I understand you say that they were going to hire him or they were not going to hire him. I was... Specifically footnote 4 the opinion says that they would have hired him but for this. The... That... That is something that I do not find any support for in the record. You think that... I find no support in the record. I find no support for it in the record. And I don't think your honor will find any support for it in the record. In New York would he have had an action against the... You say an action for a slander or defamation of some kind. There is no immunity for the police department in such an action is there? Of course there is. It is a matter of states. Well some states there is. Besides which he is not a policeman he is a former policeman. No I am talking about immunity of the defendants who got up the file. There would be no privilege for... There is no such immunity. There is no such immunity. No privilege for assembling the file a personnel file or anything like that. People who make false statements except for this. Except for the circumstance that when there is communication between a former employer and a future employer in regard to the conduct of the employer while he was in the employee of the former employer there is a limited privilege. In other words there is a privilege in so far as they communicated the information to the Pennsylvania in real life. That's right. There is a limited privilege. Well then what's this land right? But if there is but that limited privilege that limited privilege does not extend to slander and libel to unthought about to deliver to reckless statements. And again I say Valga was quite present in the courtroom and made no attempt to deny that the incident took place. But was that an issue? That wasn't an issue in the litigation. The issue in this litigation as framed by the pleadings was whether or not in such circumstances a pre-determination hearing was essential in order to dismiss a non-tenured employee who had no property right in his job. All right. Let's take that as the issue. Then whether or not this happened wasn't an issue at all in this litigation. Whether or not what you want? Whether or not this actually happened or the circumstances under which it happened if it did were not at all issues in this litigation. Yeah but by narrowing the issue in that way do you foreclose the rational inquiry? So what we're talking about here we're not dealing with something that is academic. Well you talk about his failure to take the stand and deny or explain that that was not an issue in this litigation at all was it? Well of course it wasn't. It was removed from the litigation by the circumstance that he never denied it. They never pretended that anything was otherwise. Well I thought the point of the litigation was to establish his right to a hearing somewhere else rather than that he should have the hearing right in the district court. His right to well it was to establish his right to a pre-termination hearing. Exactly. Well is it not even narrower than that a right to a hearing before they would put that kind of information in his file without notice to him? But you know Chief Justice what's the point of this? We're not engaged in a shirve. Well we're not trying to evaluate the point I'm trying to evaluate what his claim is. His claim is that that kind of information may not go into his file consistent with due process without giving him notice that this information is going into the file and then to have an opportunity then and there to deny it. No. A hearing is what is required in accordance with the opinion of the court of appeals. A hearing. To my mind a hearing is a hearing with a full panoply of cross-examination. I think that must be read as an opportunity for hearing not necessarily holding for hearing. That is not what I see because actually you know people always have an opportunity to say now why was I dismissed? Why did you do this to me? I can always do that. There's nothing wrong with that. That's not a complete answer because he did that and his answer was we just decided you weren't doing a good job. They gave him a very vague answer. So he did not have a right to find out the real reason. Except for this. Except you must assume that he knew what happened. He must subsume If it was false how does he know what might be in the file? How does he know? If you won't tell him and you don't as I understand the practice. Well you don't of course you don't tell him except you tell him that he was unsatisfactory. Now what the details are of course you don't tell him. You tell him he was unsatisfactory. But that doesn't respond to the Chief Justice's question. What is his protection against the possibility that you relied on a false inaccurate slanderous statement of some kind? He has none as I understand. That really isn't so because he has a right to challenge his dismissal. In an article 78 proceeding our courts are as open as any courts in the land to civil servants. They are the most litigating people in the world. Did he have a statutory right to some kind of hearing before his dismissal? No. Well then what is the right to his dismissal? He had a statutory right to review his dismissal in the event that his dismissal was for unconstitutional reasons. And he had that right in the Supreme Court. law because under our law a public official cannot act in so arbitrary and unreasonable manner or unconstitutional manner to discharge anybody. Even a probationary employee? I thought the law was... A probationary employee can be dismissed at will. For any reason. With reason or without reason. Any reason. But he cannot be dismissed for a reason which violates his constitutional rights. He cannot be dismissed for exercising his right of free speech. He cannot be dismissed because he was a black or because he was a Jew or for any of those reasons that are permitted under our Constitution. And for that he can get relief in our own courts. And to the extent in addition to that, that the reasons asserted for his dismissal were disgraceful or unpleasant or libelous, he has his right of action in surrender. The privilege you referred to a moment ago, Mr. Richland, that an employer has work communicating information from a former employer receiving, is that any different for a government employer than it is for a private employer under the law of the state of New York in a defamation case? No different. It is no different. Our files are even more open than the files of private firms. I was talking about the privilege that could be claimed in a defamation. Oh, certainly not. I don't think anyone has suggested that there is a, that there is a, that that a, that a, an ordinary employee who holds his job in private industry at will cannot be dismissed for any reason at all, except a reason which of course insults the Constitution. Well, no, what I'm talking about is supposing that an employee brings an action for defamation, a slander, against an, a former employer for divulging the reason for which that employee was discharged. Now, you said earlier that there's a privilege under New York law, apparently a qualified privilege, that can be asserted in telling, in effect passing along a recommendation. And my question is, is that any different, is the privilege any different for a governmental employer than it is for a private employer? I submit that it should not be. I asked you, do you know what it is? I submit that it isn't. What is the relief that you understand the Second Circuit opinion has given? I can only, I can only take the interpretation that is provided in the respondent's brief, and that is reinstatement with full pay and council fees. I take it you can't understand especially the reinstatement part of it. I can understand none of it, you hon. We have already been buried under applications for council fees in a variety of cases. You've got 800 lawyers, don't take care of us. We cannot take care of the council fees of our adversaries. And they've become a very serious problem. I just find glancing through the record that there is a mention about the Plainfield, New Jersey job that he was denied. That's right. But there's nothing in there that shows that he... Before you and I get to argue about what's in there, let's read it. rather than interpret it, huh? Of course. Thank you. And I was called by the Plainfield, New Jersey Police Department. And I was called down there for a pre-appointment interview. And I also filled out a personal history questionnaire. And I was told that the hiring date would be three weeks if the investigation was successfully completed. But I was never called back. Never called down for hiring. So he is in there. And he received a letter wishing him success in the future and I suggest that that does not raise to the level of proof of any success. Have you ever turned down somebody and wrote a nice letter saying you wish you success with someplace else? Not from the police department. Mr. Richland, let me ask a question, please. Do you understand the respondent here to concede that he had no right not to be terminated? That he concede that he had no right not to be terminated? I have too many negatives in there. I don't know. I hate to argue my adversary's case. I don't think that he takes that position. But that is what the law of this New York state is. that a probationary employee can be dismissed at any time during his probationary period. Well, I'll certainly ask your adversary, but if he were to concede this, then I wonder where this reinstatement business comes from. It's not a question for you. I wonder too, Your Honor. I wonder too. I find this a strange case. I find this a strange extension of what was said in the opinions of this court rather than what was decided in the opinions of this court. And I suggest that the decisions of this court, particularly Bishop and Paul, preclude anything but a reversal in this case, unless starry decisis lasts less than a year. Unless there are any further questions, I would like to reserve a few minutes for any reply that I think might be necessary. Very well, Mr. Richland. Mr. Rasmikoff. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. Before I proceed, if I may take one moment to introduce co-counsel, Mr. Rappaport, chief counsel, to the Patrolman's Benevolent Association, and Mr. Joe Frost, of counsel, to the PBA, I was all set after listening to my young friend's argument about there was nothing in the record pertaining to Plainfield, and Mr. Justice Marshall referred to this particular part, which of course, that was the basis why Judge Clark made that footnote number four, so that it was in the record and once Plainfield, once they went down and saw what had happened, allegedly, they wouldn't touch this man with a ten-foot pole. Who am I representing in this proceeding? A young man, 23 years of age, a brilliant boy, passes all, he's interested in law enforcement, he's a student at the John Jay Criminal College, good record, never been involved in any difficulty of any kind, he takes this examination, patrolman, police trainee, in 1970, he's only 19 years of age, passes that, he gets a mark of about 88, appointed, under that announcement for that examination, and my friend speaks of him as a provisional, as a probationer, no tenure, with nothing, that announcement stated that once he acquires, once he attains the age of 21, he becomes a patrolman. he serves two years as a police trainee, he becomes of age 21 on August 8th of 72, and on August 15th he becomes a patrolman. and then in 1973, February 73, he gets a letter with no notification of any kind, your services are unsatisfactory, and he's terminated, having spent several hundred dollars for equipment, school, and everything else, he doesn't know why. He's interested in law enforcement. Well, are you telling us he was not a probationer at that time, that he had tenure? No, no, there was some question as pointed out, the announcement isn't clear, but we'll proceed on the theory that he's serving a period of probation, even though he has been continuously employed by the police department for more than two years. Let's say he's on probation. Trainees are in quite a different capacity. They're not peace officers. They're not peace officers, that's right. Otherwise, they do all the investigative work and everything else, except they don't carry a gun, and they're not a peace officer. He's terminated. He's interested in law enforcement, safe files, government jobs, state jobs, city jobs, passes 97% of them with marks in excess of 88, 90%, and as your honors know, when a man applies for civil, in the government, where were you employed? Were you ever discharged? And so he has to state what he did. I was working for the city of New York for a period of three years. were you terminated? Yes. I don't know. He doesn't know why. Nobody's told him. We didn't know why until the time of the trial in the district court. What did the letter say? The letter says your services are unsatisfactory. Isn't that a reason? That's no reason, judge. What does that mean? Could it be attendance? Could it be in support? We don't know. Well, I should say it means in ordinary language, daily conversation or newspapers, that it's unsatisfactory. Unsatisfactory in what respect? Did he ask for a bill of particulars? They don't give bill of particulars. Well, did he ask? No, you're dealing with a young man 22 years aboard bill of particulars. They think he's out of his mind. Who'd pay attention to him, judge? Nobody would pay attention to him. So he doesn't know of anything. Would it be unreasonable to expect that a highly intelligent, as you say, 19-year-old would not have sense enough to say why? Just one word. He goes down there, he went down there, they wouldn't answer him, they don't answer him. Did he ask why? This is the standard letter that goes out. Did he ask why? He went down to the clerk's office, nobody gave him a reason. Did he ask why? From what I understand, he went, he didn't write, if that's what you mean. Did he ask why? The answer is no. Thank you. He brings this suit, after he files applications, he's not being appointed, and he finally gets himself a job in a private sector as a private security man for the Pennsylvania Railroad in New York. He's working there, serving his probationary period, he's asked the question, where were you employed? He says, police department. Were you terminated? Yes, I don't know why. They write a letter, the Penn Central writes a letter to the police department, they say, will you come on down, look at the records. Man comes out, looks at the records, and he's terminated. We bring the action, I meet these men in the court for the first time, never seen them before, and I'm hearing for the first time, what all this is all about. And then we hear, one of the men says, he looked at the records, four or five men were involved, there was some statement to the fact, that, let me read the exact testimony, it's 81A, did you ever sign an authorization for the police department, no, on page 89A of the record, what happened after he looked at the records? I drew a negative attitude from the New York City Police Department, they advised me to go about it by letter, I explained to them what I already attempted to do by letter, I gave up. Question, as a police officer, were you satisfied with that report? Answer, no sir, question, they wouldn't permit you to investigate or talk to these other policemen that were involved there, the other probationary patrolmen, is that correct? No, they wouldn't permit it, I just drew a blank attitude from the New York City Police Department, I decided that I could never prove or disprove exactly what happened, so I let it go as it stood, then what happened, I went back, reported, and the man was terminated. Now, during the course of the oral argument, Judge Clark, Mr. Reznikoff, before you get to the oral argument, you mentioned the first you heard of this was at the trial. That is correct. You're familiar with the pre-trial discovery procedures that the federal rules authorize, are you not? Yes, we didn't, they wouldn't give it to us. You asked the question why, and they gave you an evasive answer. They said you're not entitled to it. Did you follow up that in any way with asking the judge for a more complete answer? No. Because you would have been entitled to it, I think. We asked for it, they gave us that, and that was that, and we pointed that out before Judge Garfine, and before Judge But you did make no further attempt to find out. Judge Clark, during the course of the oral argument, my young friend here, Mr. Richland, did not argue a woman, a woman argued the appeal there, and Mr. Justice Clark asked the woman, supposing in that letter, which conceitedly was untruthful, that that was not a correct letter that should have gone out because his services were satisfactory. Which letter are you now referring to? You're saying that the letter of termination that went out that says your services are unsatisfactory. And Judge Clark said... Well, now, wait a minute. You characterize that as an untruthful letter? Yeah, well, in the sense that his services as an employee were satisfactory, there was no question. He had never been served with any charges. He had never been found guilty of anything other than this one incident which allegedly took place in the police academy. Other than that, there was nothing, nothing of anything derogatory about this man. Well, how can you know that? Well, there was nothing in the record. Well, does it have a probationary employee? Does it have to be in the record? Well, normally a man serving the probation and the police department, they serve him with charges. They have hearings there in the police department. They have hearings. They give a man hearing in the police department. Well, then you're saying it's New York practice that unless there has been a hearing for a probationary employee, the supervisor could not respond to a request such as this, telling an employee he'd been discharged because his services were unsatisfactory? They have never, and in my vast experience that I've had with police department in the city, they have never indicated to a man other than the standard letter which goes out, which says your services have been found to be unsatisfactory. As far as the police department is concerned, that is the end of the matter. So this is a standard letter. This is a standard letter. That's right. And Judge Clark said to counsel, if they had indicated the truth which they thought was so in that letter that this man allegedly put a gun to his head, would he have been entitled to a hearing? Was that a stigma? Would that have been a stigma? And corporation counsel said yes. Said yes. So then Judge Clark says, well, that's the case. Doesn't it work out that way when somebody goes and looks at this man's record and sees something about a gun? What law enforcement agency is going to imply, would employ this man? There's no answer to that. As Mr. Justice Marshall points out, why should this young man, 23 years of age, go through the rest of his life with an indication of this kind, this kind of a stigma, that he attempted suicide, when it never happened, he doesn't know anything about it, and they have made a mountain out of a molehill here because I, during colloquy, before the judge in the district court, I said, it might have been a little horseplay between four or five young men in the academy at the time, at the police, that's the only time it appeared in the record, there is no testimony about anything like this, they had an opportunity to do that, they could have come forward with that, but they never did. Well, are you two saying that it should have, that this hearing should have taken place right in the district court? I understood your opponent to contend that, and several of us thought that was not the case. Well, as long as there was a hearing, Judge Reckless, in the district court, I said it was incumbent upon them at least to come forward with some evidence, or at least make an offer of proof, that what they allege, or what appears to be in some record of some kind, actually happened.
